ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, the pentagon $ABCDE$ is a regular pentagon. If $l_{1} \parallel l_{2}$, then what is the value of $\angle \alpha - \angle \beta$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution} Let line $BF$ pass through point $B$ and be parallel to $l_{1}$, as shown in the figure:\\
Since $l_{1}\parallel l_{2}$,\\
it follows that $BF\parallel l_{1}\parallel l_{2}$,\\
thus, $\angle \beta =\angle CBF$ and $\angle ABF+\angle \alpha =180^\circ$,\\
therefore, $\angle \alpha =180^\circ-\angle ABF$,\\
also, since pentagon $ABCDE$ is a regular pentagon,\\
it follows that $\angle ABC=\frac{180^\circ\times (5-2)}{5}=108^\circ$,\\
also, since $\angle ABC=\angle ABF+\angle CBF$,\\
it follows that $108^\circ=\angle \beta +180^\circ-\angle \alpha$\\
therefore, $\angle \alpha -\angle \beta =\boxed{72^\circ}$.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as a regular pentagon ABCDE with the upper line l1 crossing side AB and the lower line l2 crossing side BC; alpha is the angle made by AB with l1, and beta is the angle made by BC with l2. Draw an auxiliary line through B parallel to l1 and l2. By corresponding angles, beta equals the angle between BC and this auxiliary parallel. Also, the angle between BA and the auxiliary parallel is supplementary to alpha, so it is 180° - alpha. Since ABCDE is regular, the interior angle at B is 108°, and this interior angle is the sum of those two angles: (180° - alpha) + beta = 108°. Rearranging gives alpha - beta = 72°.

ready3_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, the pentagon $ABCDE$ is a regular pentagon. If $l_{1} \parallel l_{2}$, then what is the value of $\angle \alpha - \angle \beta$?
ready3_open_rewrite.raw_answer:
\textbf{Solution} Let line $BF$ pass through point $B$ and be parallel to $l_{1}$, as shown in the figure:\\
Since $l_{1}\parallel l_{2}$,\\
it follows that $BF\parallel l_{1}\parallel l_{2}$,\\
thus, $\angle \beta =\angle CBF$ and $\angle ABF+\angle \alpha =180^\circ$,\\
therefore, $\angle \alpha =180^\circ-\angle ABF$,\\
also, since pentagon $ABCDE$ is a regular pentagon,\\
it follows that $\angle ABC=\frac{180^\circ\times (5-2)}{5}=108^\circ$,\\
also, since $\angle ABC=\angle ABF+\angle CBF$,\\
it follows that $108^\circ=\angle \beta +180^\circ-\angle \alpha$\\
therefore, $\angle \alpha -\angle \beta =\boxed{72^\circ}$.
